name: Spontaneity Arete
overview: A six-pitch (plus optional 7th) 5.7 alpine rock route climbing the long, prominent arête of Le Petit Cheval; short, well-protected cruxes are broken up by long scrambling sections between pitches, giving it an alpine-adventure feel more than a sustained rock outing.
beta: A moderate but long day: cracks off a snag, a traverse under a roof (the 'Pac Man' pitch), steepening ground with cracks, a 10-inch finger/hand crack, a liebacking corner crack, and a finishing headwall pitch (the 'Goldie Crack' variation is a highlight) lead to the summit area. Reviews are mixed — some call it a classic alpine day, others find the scrambling between pitches makes it feel long for the climbing delivered.
descent_text: Most parties rappel the line of the route, which some report takes a long time (about 9 rappels, with occasional rope snags on flakes requiring re-ascent to free them). The alternative is descending the 3rd-class gully climber's right of the route, which is faster but described as loose and 'gnarly' — staying high and skier's-right reduces exposure to looseness.
descent: Rappel the route (60m rope) or downclimb/descend the loose gully to climber's right.
rappels: Rappel the route on a 60 m rope: about five or six rappels to the base of the third pitch, or about nine all the way down, with occasional rope snags on flakes. The faster alternative is the loose 3rd-class gully climber’s right of the route.

pitch_detail.notes: Where the lower ridge steepens into upper 5th class at a few trees, traverse left onto the more exposed side of the ridge. Find a snag beside a vertical #3-size crack. Climb cracks from the snag, including a short hand crack with 5.7 moves, to a belay just below the roof.

The 'Pac Man' pitch. Traverse out right under the roof, passing beneath its right side (going up and left over it is harder), and continue about 50 ft beyond. This pitch takes the most gear, and some parties find it the hardest. Above, scramble roughly ten minutes of class 3 up the ridge to the next steepening. The way on is not obvious here, and the gully alongside is loose.

Start on the steepening ground and follow cracks, belaying where comfortable or at the base of a 10-inch-wide crack. Parties often link pitches 3 to 5 into two. Some belay 20–30 ft past the fixed rap anchors for better stances.
Short start up the 10-inch crack, with gear in cracks to its left. Above it, follow finger and hand cracks past a shallow gully and some bushes to a belay on a flat section.

Either take the corner crack to the right or the cracks straight above to a tree, then lieback the corner the tree grows in. Above the corner, easier ground leads to the next steepening of the ridge. Much of this pitch is easier than the others.
Follow cracks up to lower-angle ground and belay below the final headwall, which has a #3-size crack out to the left. Pitches 6 and 7 are the best-regarded on the route.

Short, excellent leaning crack on the left that takes #3-size cams, only two or three pieces. The easier option is the blocky trough and gully to its right: walk a short ledge to an exposed step, then climb a second steep groove.

About 200–300 ft of class 3 along the crest, with an exposed 4th-class move near the summit. Topping out commits the party to descending the loose gully climber's right of the route. From the summit one rappel reaches that gully.
